feedback.problem: Find the $x$-coordinate of the point of inflection for $f(x)={e}^{x}({x}^{2}-4x+7).$
feedback.worked_solution:
For continuous, twice-differentiable functions, we can determine possible points of inflection by solving the equation ${f}^{″}(x)=0.$ However, we must be sure to check that the concavity does indeed change at whatever points we find.

First, we calculate the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={e}^{x}({x}^{2}-4x+7)+{e}^{x}(2x-4) \\  & ={e}^{x}({x}^{2}-2x+3) \\ {f}^{″}(x) & ={e}^{x}({x}^{2}-2x+3)+{e}^{x}(2x-2) \\  & ={e}^{x}({x}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we solve ${f}^{″}(x)=0.$

Since ${e}^{x}({x}^{2}+1)>0$ for all real values of $x,$ the equation ${f}^{″}(x)=0$ has no real solutions, and so there are no points of inflection.

submitted_fields.submitted_value: There are no points of inflection
